posts.text: Every snake care sheet warns you about humidity running too low. For a rosy boa that advice is backwards, and it is why most of them get sick.
comments: This is a desert species. Excess ambient moisture is the primary trigger for respiratory infection here, not dryness. Nasal discharge, wheezing, open-mouth breathing, lethargy.
Scale rot comes from the same root cause, damp or dirty substrate. Discolored belly scales, sometimes with an odor.
The fix is keeping dry aspen substrate genuinely dry rather than letting it sit damp between changes, and a hygrometer to confirm the enclosure holds this species' unusually low target.
Full guide on the humidity reversal and the rest of the health list here → https://beastlyfacts.com/blog/rosy-boa-health-issues-guide/

posts.text: Red-footed tortoises break the rule every other tortoise guide on this site teaches. Keep one the way you would keep a Russian tortoise and you will make it sick.
comments: For an arid species, damp and cold cause respiratory infection. For a red-foot it is the reverse, chronically dry and cool conditions are the risk.
Reptile vets describe a red-footed tortoise kept dry and cool as highly likely to eventually develop respiratory problems. Wheezing, nasal discharge, lethargy, open-mouth breathing.
It does not resolve on its own and needs antibiotics, so vet first, then raise humidity and warmth while you wait. What are you actually running for humidity on yours?
Full guide on the reversal and the rest of the health list here → https://beastlyfacts.com/blog/red-footed-tortoise-health-issues-guide/

posts.text: Mice are hardy for their size, right up until they are not. The thing that kills them moves faster than most owners expect.
comments: Most serious mouse respiratory disease traces to Mycoplasma pulmonis, the same pathogen behind chronic respiratory disease in pet rats. Highly contagious, and it can sit asymptomatic a long stretch before flaring.
Watch for sneezing, nasal or eye discharge, labored or noisy breathing, a hunched posture, ruffled coat, reduced activity.
Damp, drafts, dust, and poor ventilation all raise the risk. Merck's comfort range is 64 to 79F and 30 to 70% humidity, which is worth actually measuring rather than guessing.
Full guide on respiratory risk and the rest of the health list here → https://beastlyfacts.com/blog/mouse-health-issues-guide/

posts.text: Nearly every pet rat has it. Most owners do not know what they are looking at until it is well underway.
comments: Merck calls chronic respiratory disease, caused by Mycoplasma pulmonis, the most common health problem in rats. A survey of pet ratteries in the northwestern US found 95% of them positive for it.
Watch for sneezing, sniffling, noisy breathing, a rough coat, lethargy, weight loss, head tilt, and reddish-brown porphyrin staining around the eyes and nose.

There is no cure. Antibiotics ease a flare-up, and Merck is blunt that rats with the chronic form rarely live past 2 years. Cage ammonia from infrequent cleaning is a documented driver, which makes housing quality the real lever.
Full breakdown on flare-ups and the rest of the health list here → https://beastlyfacts.com/blog/rat-health-issues-guide/

posts.text: Parrotlets have a big parrot personality in a tiny body, and that is exactly what makes the health side harder than people expect.
comments: They hide illness like every prey bird does, and their size means a problem advances faster than it would in a larger parrot. Tail-bobbing with each breath, open-mouth breathing, fluffed appearance.
Avian vets treat respiratory signs as a same-day emergency until proven otherwise. A bird's respiratory system can deteriorate quickly once symptoms are visible at all.
Feather plucking is the other one, and boredom hits this species harder than most. Real cage space and rotating forage toys address that side, but a vet rules out medical causes first.
Full guide on what to watch for here → https://beastlyfacts.com/blog/parrotlet-health-issues-guide/

posts.text: Zebra finches are a prey species that hides illness well, so the conditions worth knowing are the ones you will not notice on your own.
comments: Air sac mites live in the trachea and air sacs. Mild infections are often asymptomatic, but heavy ones bring audible high-pitched noises and clicking, sneezing, tail bobbing, open-mouthed breathing.

Egg binding is the other emergency. Merck lists sitting on the cage floor, weakness, straining, bloody droppings, a sudden stop in laying, and a swollen abdomen, with calcium deficiency named as a key cause.
Which is exactly why a cuttlebone is not an optional extra for a laying hen. Does yours have constant access to one?
Full guide on mites, egg binding, and the rest here → https://beastlyfacts.com/blog/zebra-finch-health-issues-guide/

posts.text: Cherry shrimp do not usually die of disease. They die of a molt that went wrong, and by the time you see it there is nothing to do.
comments: An adult sheds roughly every 3 to 4 weeks. A failed molt shows as the white ring of death, a complete white band around the middle of the body instead of a clean split at the head.
It usually traces to a rapid swing in general hardness, an oversized or sudden water change, a calcium and protein poor diet, or water simply too cold to support a normal molt.
It is usually fatal once it happens, so the leverage is entirely on prevention: stable GH, gradual water changes, a properly fed colony.
Full guide on GH targets and the rest of the health list here → https://beastlyfacts.com/blog/cherry-shrimp-health-issues-guide/

posts.text: A bristlenose pleco living on tank algae alone is slowly starving, and it takes months before it looks like anything at all.
comments: It shows as a sunken, concave belly developing over weeks or months, sometimes with faded color or fins that look ragged without an infection driving it.
This is the single most common and most damaging condition for the species precisely because it is gradual. There is no obvious symptom on day one.
The fix is a real diet, sinking wafers and vegetables as the staple rather than whatever grows on the glass. What are you actually feeding yours?
Full guide on the real diet and the rest of the health list here → https://beastlyfacts.com/blog/bristlenose-pleco-health-issues-guide/

posts.text: Discus have a reputation for being delicate. Most of what backs that up is not fragility, it is a much narrower margin for error than other fish give you.
comments: Ich shows as small white spots on skin and gills, usually after flashing against decor, weakness, and appetite loss. Temperature swings are the most frequently named trigger.
Treatment goes higher than standard advice here, toward roughly 90F rather than the 82 to 86F this species already lives at, because discus have less headroom before hitting ich's own survival limit.
Daily 50% water changes in quarantine plus a copper, formalin, or potassium permanganate treatment round it out.
Full guide on water targets and the rest of the health list here → https://beastlyfacts.com/blog/discus-health-issues-guide/

posts.text: Flying squirrel health comes down to diet more than almost anything else, and the failure mode looks exactly like the sugar glider's.
comments: Metabolic bone disease is the most common serious issue, and it is almost entirely diet driven. A calcium-poor, phosphorus-heavy diet built too heavily on nuts, seeds, and acorns is how it happens.
The target calcium to phosphorus ratio is roughly 2 to 1. Watch for lethargy, reduced appetite, and reluctance to climb early, progressing to hind-limb weakness, tremors, fractures, and seizures.
Prevention is the whole game here, because by the time the late signs show up you are already deep into it.
Full guide on the diet correction and the rest of the health list here → https://beastlyfacts.com/blog/flying-squirrel-health-issues-guide/

posts.text: Jackson's chameleons get sold as a beginner-friendly step up from a veiled. Same core failure mode, and it is the one that ends most of them.
comments: Metabolic bone disease, from inadequate calcium, vitamin D3, or UVB. Lethargy, rubbery or bent bones, swollen limbs, tremors.
Early cases respond considerably better to treatment than advanced ones, and this is a species where advanced usually means permanent.
Dehydration sits right behind it, since chameleons drink moving droplets rather than from a standing bowl. What is your misting or dripper routine?
Full guide on MBD and the rest of the health list here → https://beastlyfacts.com/blog/jacksons-chameleon-health-issues-guide/

posts.text: Hissing cockroaches are about as hardy as a pet gets. Almost everything that goes wrong is one number being off.
comments: Low humidity causes real molting problems and can kill if left uncorrected. Everything on the health list traces back to humidity or basic enclosure hygiene.
The target is 60 to 70%, held with regular misting and a moisture-holding coconut fiber substrate rather than whatever the enclosure happens to sit at.
That is genuinely most of the care. Get the number right and the rest of the list mostly stops applying.
Full guide on humidity and molting here → https://beastlyfacts.com/blog/madagascar-hissing-cockroach-health-issues-guide/

posts.text: Lovebirds hide illness so well that by the time you notice, it is usually further along than it would be in almost any other pet.
comments: Lovebirds are particularly susceptible to psittacine beak and feather disease, a virus that attacks feather and beak cells along with the immune system. Feather deformities, feather loss, beak abnormalities.
It is often fatal, has no cure, and is highly contagious between birds.
Which makes testing any new bird before introducing it to an existing one genuine prevention rather than excessive caution.
Full guide on PBFD and the rest of the health list here → https://beastlyfacts.com/blog/lovebird-health-issues-guide/

posts.text: Tokay geckos are hardy, loud, and famously willing to bite. The thing that actually hurts them is quieter than any of that.
comments: Metabolic bone disease. A soft or rubbery jaw, tremors, difficulty gripping or climbing, visible deformities, and it tends to be worse in juveniles.
Caused by low calcium or vitamin D3 and insufficient UVB, which makes it a setup problem rather than a bad-luck problem.
Correct UVB and calcium supplementation are the two levers that prevent it before it starts. Parasites are the other one to know, especially in wild-caught animals.
Full guide on UVB, calcium, and the rest here → https://beastlyfacts.com/blog/tokay-gecko-health-issues-guide/
